title: QUANTUM RESERVOIR COMPUTING FOR CREDIT CARD DEFAULT PREDICTION ON A NEUTRAL ATOM PLATFORM
abstract_summary: The paper implements and benchmarks a hybrid quantum-classical machine learning pipeline that incorporates a Quantum Reservoir Computing (QRC) layer executed on QuEra's 256-qubit Aquila neutral-atom simulator, using position and local-detuning encodings. The method is applied to a real-world imbalanced credit card default prediction dataset and compared against classical baselines (including a DNN); noiseless emulation achieves competitive performance while real-hardware noise notably degrades results, though QRC shows promise in flexibility and scalability for future applications.
methodology_description: The authors implemented and benchmarked a hybrid quantum-classical classification pipeline for credit-card default prediction. The pipeline consists of three main stages: (1) preprocessing of the public UCI 'Default of Credit Card Clients' dataset (cleaning, scaling to [-1,+1], one-hot encoding of categorical variables, PCA retaining 11 principal components, hierarchical clustering of features into 12 groups and aggregation by averaging to produce 12 input features); (2) a reservoir computing layer (either Quantum Reservoir Computing (QRC) executed on a neutral-atom analog simulator or a classical reservoir computing (CRC) dequantized spin model) that maps the aggregated features into a higher-dimensional feature space; and (3) a classical classification stage using simple fast-to-train classifiers (KNN, SGD, Gaussian Naïve Bayes, Logistic Regression, Perceptron, linear SVM) combined with resampling methods (SMOTE, K-means SMOTE, Cluster Centroids, or none). The QRC encodes the 12 preprocessed features using two encoding strategies on a neutral-atom platform: position encoding (mapping features to inter-atomic distances) and local-detuning encoding (mapping features to local detuning amplitudes). For each sample the reservoir output is formed by time-series measurements of single-site expectations ⟨Zi⟩ and pairwise correlations ⟨ZiZj⟩ computed across 5 timesteps, producing 390 (detuning) or 455 (position) features in total. Emulation of the quantum dynamics was performed using Bloqade.jl (statevector and shot-based simulations) to tune parameters and set shot counts; subsequent experiments were run on QuEra’s Aquila 256-qubit neutral-atom simulator. Baselines include the CRC dequantized reservoir, a fully-classical pipeline (preprocessing + classifiers), and a Deep Neural Network (DNN) benchmark (6-layer fully connected network trained with Adam). Evaluation focused on F1-score for the imbalanced classification task and also recorded training times. The study also examined the impact of hardware noise by comparing noiseless statevector emulation, shot-based emulation, and real-device results.
algorithms_used: Classical Reservoir Computing (CRC) - dequantized spin model
Stochastic Gradient Descent classifier (SGD / linear hinge loss)
experimental_setup: Analog neutral-atom QPU (QuEra Aquila) and classical emulation (Bloqade.jl). Aquila: 256-qubit neutral-atom simulator supporting local detuning, 2D register 75 µm × 125 µm, minimum vertical spacing 4 µm. QRC pulse sequences: 5 timesteps of 0.5 µs each (total per-sample measurement sequence simulated by restarting initial state each timestep), steep ramp up/down of 0.05 µs, maximum Rabi frequency Ωmax = 2π rad/µs. Inter-atomic base spacing r0 = 10 µm. Position encoding scale λ tuned (optimal λ = 1.0 reported); detuning encoding used ∆global = π rad/µs (emulation) and ∆global = 2.0 rad/µs used in some position tuning. Emulation performed both as statevector and shot-based; an optimal shot budget n_opt = 240 shots per sample (40 shots per timestep) chosen with N_repl = 6 replicated arrays per register to increase sampling. Measurements collected: expectation values ⟨Zi⟩ and ⟨ZiZj⟩ per timestep to form reservoir output.
dataset_used: UCI Machine Learning Repository: 'Default of Credit Card Clients' dataset (Taiwan). Original dataset: 30,000 samples with 23 features + binary default label. After cleaning (removal of small number of samples with undocumented category values) the used dataset contained 29,601 samples (referred to as CARDS_30000). Two smaller stratified subsets were used for hardware runs: CARDS_2500 (≈2,571 samples) and CARDS_1000 (1,000 samples).

experiment_input.source: UCI Machine Learning Repository, 'Default of Credit Card Clients' (Yeh, 2009)
preprocessing_steps: Remove samples with undocumented categorical values (MARRIAGE, EDUCATION)
One-hot encoding for SEX and MARRIAGE
Hierarchical clustering in PCA space to aggregate 24 features into 12 clusters
Aggregate features inside each cluster by averaging to produce 12 features

pipeline_steps: Preprocessing as above to produce 12 aggregated features per sample
- Detuning encoding: map each of 12 features to local detuning amplitude ∆i = ∆global + ∆l * f_i (requires n = 12 atoms)
- Position encoding: map features to inter-atomic displacements ri,i+1 = r0(1 + λ f_i) (requires n+1 atoms = 13 atoms)

Time evolution under Aquila effective Hamiltonian H(t) (Ω(t), ϕ(t), ∆i(t), Van der Waals interactions Vij), for 5 timesteps of 0.5 μs each; reset to |0...0⟩ and rerun per timestep on real device (non-destructive measurement not available)
Observe and record single-site expectations ⟨Zi⟩ and pairwise ⟨ZiZj⟩ for all pairs per timestep to form reservoir feature vector (78 features per timestep for detuning; 91 for position)
Aggregate across 5 timesteps to final reservoir features (390 detuning, 455 position)

Classical classification stage: apply resampling to training set (None/SMOTE/K-SMOTE/ClusterCentroids) then train classifiers (KNN, SGD, NB, Logistic, Perceptron, linear SVM) with hyperparameter grid search optimizing F1 on validation set
Compare to CRC (classical spin emulation of same Hamiltonian dynamics) and a DNN baseline trained directly on the 12 preprocessed features
parameter_search_and_tuning: Position encoding: tuned λ (optimal reported λ=1.0) and ∆global (optimal reported ∆global=2.0 rad/µs)
Detuning encoding: ∆global explored in [0,9] rad/µs; chosen ∆global = π rad/µs in emulation
Shot budget exploration (statevector vs shot-based emulation) led to selection of n_opt = 240 shots per sample (40 shots per timestep) and N_repl = 6 replicas on-device
Classifiers hyperparameter grids: K for KNN in {2..15}; SGD epochs {10,20,..,100}; Logistic C in {1e-3,...,1e2}; Perceptron η in {1e-1,1e-2,1e-3}; SVM C in {1e-1,1e2,1e1,1e2} (as reported)
iterations: DNN trained for up to 1000 epochs with early stopping (patience 30); grid search on learning rate {0.1,0.01,0.001} and batch size {64,128,256}
Classical emulation runs and parameter sweeps using Bloqade.jl to set pulse/encoding parameters and shot counts prior to hardware execution

metrics_reported: Statistical correlation between Aquila QRC features and shot-based/statevector emulation across timesteps
Comparison of statevector emulation, shot-based emulation, and Aquila real-device performance
baselines: Deep Neural Network trained on preprocessed features

key_findings: [supported] Implemented a hybrid quantum-classical pipeline that inserts a Quantum Reservoir Computing (QRC) layer (emulated and on QuEra Aquila) between classical preprocessing and classical classifiers for binary credit-card-default prediction.
[supported] Executed QRC using two encodings on a neutral-atom platform: position encoding (data → inter-atomic distances) and detuning encoding (data → local detuning amplitudes).

[supported] Generated reservoir output feature vectors consisting of single-qubit expectations and pairwise correlations: detuning encoding yields 78 features per timestep (390 features for 5 timesteps); position encoding yields 91 features per timestep (455 features for 5 timesteps).

[supported] Noiseless classical statevector emulation of the QRC achieves classification performance comparable to a fully-classical Deep Neural Network (DNN) baseline on the tested credit-card dataset.

[supported] Hardware noise on Aquila significantly degrades QRC-derived classification performance relative to noiseless emulation; correlation between emulation and hardware degrades with later timesteps (decoherence effects).

[supported] Detuning encoding performs better than or comparable to position encoding on real Aquila hardware in the experiments reported (likely because of lower shot-to-shot fluctuation in detuning vs atom positioning).

[supported] Shot-count experiments (emulation and hardware) show F1 performance plateaus after a few hundred Hamiltonian simulations; based on replication strategy (N_repl=6) the authors chose n_opt = 240 total shots (≈40 shots per timestep) as a trade-off.

[supported] Using QRC output features, simple classifiers (KNN, Naïve Bayes, Logistic Model, Perceptron, SGD-based linear models) train substantially faster than the implemented DNN in the reported experiments; SVM training time is an exception and becomes prohibitive at the high reservoir dimensionalities used.

[supported] On smaller datasets run on hardware (CARDS_1000, CARDS_2500) classification scores from statevector emulation exceed those from real-device runs, but hardware results approach emulation as sample size increases.
[speculative] The QRC approach (especially on neutral-atom analog hardware) is flexible and scalable and thus has strong potential for a wide range of applications beyond the present benchmark.

[speculative] Hybrid quantum-classical QRC approaches may be advantageous in practice because they keep training light (only the classical output layer) and could tolerate limited data availability (reservoir computing often requires fewer data), enabling faster/cheaper training pipelines.
[speculative] Aquila was reported as the only publicly accessible neutral-atom platform with local detuning access at the time of the experiments (authors' knowledge statement).
results_summary: The authors developed and benchmarked a hybrid quantum-classical classification pipeline that uses a Quantum Reservoir Computing (QRC) layer (implemented in emulation and on QuEra's Aquila neutral-atom simulator) for credit-card default prediction. They tested two encoding schemes (position and local detuning), reduced input dimensionality via PCA and feature aggregation, and fed reservoir-derived features into simple classical classifiers and a DNN baseline. In noiseless emulation the QRC-derived features yield classification F1 scores comparable to a DNN while enabling substantially faster training for many simple classifiers. Running on real hardware, performance falls behind emulation due to decoherence and noise; detuning encoding is generally more robust than position encoding on Aquila. The work reports concrete engineering choices (pulse timing, shot budget, replica strategy) and indicates QRC's potential scalability on neutral-atom platforms, while not demonstrating a practical quantum advantage on the studied task due to current hardware noise.
performance_claims: Detuning QRC (statevector emulation) on CARDS_30000: best reported per-figure reference F1 ~0.57 for SGD classifier (label in Figure 6: 'Max (SGD - QRC detuning sv - None): 0.57') [supported].
CARDS_1000 (statevector detuning + kSMOTE): best reported per-figure reference F1 = 0.71 (label in Figure 9: 'Max (SVM - QRC detuning sv - kSMOTE): 0.71') [supported].
CARDS_2500 (reported best of plotted configurations): example label shows 'Max (SVM - CRC - None): 0.63' F1 in Figure 12 [supported].

Reservoir feature dimensionality: detuning encoding → 78 features per timestep (12 input features → 78 including pairwise terms), 78×5=390 features for 5 timesteps; position encoding → 91 per timestep, 91×5=455 features for 5 timesteps [supported].

Shot-count plateau: performance stabilizes after a few hundred Hamiltonian simulations; authors selected n_opt = 240 shots (40 shots per timestep with 6 replicas) as operational choice on Aquila [supported].

Training times (CARDS_30000): KNN ≈ 0.12s (None), SGD ≈ 2.86s (None), Naïve Bayes ≈ 0.11s (None), Logistic Model ≈ 0.14s (None), Perceptron ≈ 0.18s (None), SVM ≈ 1515.93s (None); DNN ≈ 26.52s (None). Oversampling increases training time; undersampling decreases it. (Values from Table 2) [supported].

Pulse and timing choices: used 5 timesteps of 0.5 μs each in emulation; on hardware each timestep required a separate Hamiltonian simulation (due to destructive measurements), increasing effective pulse durations in hardware experiments [supported].
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper does not demonstrate a practical quantum advantage for the credit-card-default task. Noiseless QRC emulation attains performance comparable to a classical DNN, but real-device results are degraded by hardware noise and decoherence; thus no empirical quantum advantage is claimed or demonstrated. The authors instead highlight potential future scalability and flexibility of QRC on large neutral-atom hardware (speculative).
limitations: Hardware noise on Aquila significantly degrades classification performance compared to noiseless emulation (author-stated).
Limited coherence time of neutral-atom simulator constrains pulse/timestep design and contributes to decoherence at later timesteps (author-stated).
Register size and embedding constraints limit the amount of input data that can be encoded per atom array and limit achievable sampling rate via replication (author-stated).

Lack of non-destructive (weak) measurements on the platform requires restarting the QRC from the initial state for each timestep, resulting in longer total pulse durations and increased exposure to decoherence (author-stated).
Only small subsets of the full dataset were executed on the QPU (CARDS_1000 and CARDS_2500) due to limited quantum resources; full-dataset QPU evaluation was not performed (author-stated).
Position encoding is sensitive to atom-positioning fluctuations, making it more vulnerable to shot-to-shot hardware noise than detuning encoding (author-stated).
Shot noise / finite number of measurements limits fidelity of measured QRC features; increasing shots beyond a few hundred yields diminishing returns (author-stated).
Classical emulation of the quantum reservoir is computationally expensive, limiting exhaustive emulation studies (author-stated).
High-dimensional reservoir outputs can make some classical classifiers (e.g., SVM) computationally expensive or impractical to train in the QRC pipeline (author-stated).
The reported results are comparable to classical benchmarks but do not demonstrate a clear practical advantage of QRC for this specific use case (author-stated).
Feature preprocessing (PCA and aggregation) was required to reduce dimensionality before encoding, which may lose information and influences the mapping to the quantum reservoir (author-stated).
[inferred] The study uses a single public credit-card dataset; conclusions about QRC generalizability to other financial datasets and tasks are therefore limited.
[inferred] The experiments do not include advanced noise-mitigation or error-correction techniques; the impact of such techniques on closing the emulator–hardware performance gap remains untested.

[inferred] The choice of pulse shapes, scaling factors (e.g., λ, ∆global), timestep count, and other QRC hyperparameters was limited and tuned empirically; broader hyperparameter sensitivity and optimization were not fully explored.

[inferred] The analog-neutral-atom approach evaluated is platform-specific (Aquila) and relies on experimental features (local detuning); portability of the pipeline to other quantum hardware types is not established.

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — Noiseless statevector emulation of Quantum Reservoir Computing (QRC) achieves competitive F1-scores versus classical baselines and a DNN on the imbalanced credit-card default dataset, indicating potential expressive benefits of QRC feature maps.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — The study explicitly evaluates NISQ-era conditions (shot-based emulation and runs on QuEra Aquila), finding that hardware noise and finite-shot sampling notably degrade performance compared to noiseless emulation.

#idea:hybrid-approach — A practical hybrid pipeline (classical preprocessing: PCA, clustering, resampling; QRC reservoir layer; classical classifiers) is proposed and benchmarked, showing manageable training times and flexibility in combining quantum reservoirs with standard ML classifiers.

#limitation:noise — Real-device noise and sampling variance materially reduce classification performance; the paper identifies an optimal shot budget (240 shots/sample) but still reports degraded hardware results relative to ideal simulation.

#limitation:simulation-only — The strongest positive results come from noiseless emulation and simulator runs; hardware experiments are limited to smaller subsets and show poorer outcomes, so empirical quantum advantage on real QPUs is not demonstrated.
contradictions: Noiseless emulation results suggest QRC can match or beat classical baselines, but experiments incorporating real-device noise (shot-based emulation / hardware runs) show significantly degraded performance — a direct contradiction between simulated quantum advantage and practical noisy-device outcomes.

The authors claim promise for scalability and flexibility on a 256-qubit neutral-atom platform, yet the reported experiments use small atom registers (12–13 atoms) and rely heavily on simulator/emulation. Thus claims about scaling to real-world problem sizes are not empirically supported by the presented hardware data.
